nameStory: The Atlantic Coast leopard frog gets its name from the beautiful spotted pattern across its back and legs that looks remarkably like a leopard's rosettes. This frog was only recently discovered and described by scientists in 2014, making it one of the newest amphibian species known to science!
description: The Atlantic Coast leopard frog is a medium-sized true frog with the classic smooth, moist skin you'd expect from pond-dwelling amphibians. Like other leopard frogs, it sports distinctive dark spots scattered across its back and legs against a brownish or greenish background. These frogs have the typical frog build with a narrow waist, long powerful hind legs for jumping, and prominent eyes that help them spot both prey and predators.

idTips.label: Color/Pattern
idTips.description: Dark rounded or oval spots scattered across a brown or greenish background, creating a leopard-like pattern that's especially noticeable on the back and legs

idTips.label: Skin
idTips.description: Smooth, moist skin that feels cool and slightly slippery to the touch, typical of aquatic frogs

idTips.label: Call
idTips.description: Unique mating call that helps distinguish it from other leopard frog species, though you'll need experience with frog calls to tell the difference

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in freshwater wetlands, ponds, and slow-moving streams along the Atlantic coastal region

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Prominent golden or bronze-colored eyes that sit high on the head, allowing the frog to peer above water while mostly submerged

habitat: Look for Atlantic Coast leopard frogs in freshwater wetlands, ponds, marshes, and slow-moving streams in coastal areas of southern New England, particularly Connecticut. They prefer areas with plenty of aquatic vegetation and muddy or sandy bottoms where they can easily hide among plants or burrow slightly into soft substrate.

seasonality.spring: Breeding season begins as temperatures warm, with adults becoming active and moving to breeding pools where you might hear their calls echoing across the water.
seasonality.summer: Adults are most active and visible, often seen basking at pond edges or hunting for insects. Tadpoles develop in the water during this time.
seasonality.fall: Adults prepare for winter by feeding heavily and may begin moving toward hibernation sites as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Frogs hibernate underwater in mud at the bottom of ponds or streams, remaining dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: This frog was hiding in plain sight for decades! Scientists thought all leopard frogs in the area were Northern leopard frogs until they noticed subtle differences in calls, genetics, and habitat preferences, leading to the discovery that this was actually a completely separate species in 2014.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Northern leopard frog, which has very similar spotting patterns. The most reliable way to tell them apart is by their calls during breeding season and their preferred habitats - Atlantic Coast leopard frogs stick closer to coastal areas while Northern leopard frogs range much more widely inland.
contextualKnowledge: Because this species was only recently described in 2014, many older field guides and websites won't include it, instead lumping it in with Northern leopard frogs. This means there's still a lot scientists are learning about its exact range, behavior, and conservation needs.
compareHints: Among its leopard frog relatives, the Atlantic Coast leopard frog is most similar to the Northern leopard frog but has a more restricted coastal range. Unlike the Pickerel frog which has more rectangular spots and bright yellow or orange coloring on the inner thighs, Atlantic Coast leopard frogs have rounder spots and lack the bright warning colors. It's also smaller and more delicately built than the massive American bullfrog.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its water frog relatives, green frogs are larger than wood frogs and leopard frogs but smaller than bullfrogs, and they're the only ones that consistently show green coloring on the head.
Unlike the green frog which has prominent ridges down its back and lives near permanent water, wood frogs are smooth-backed forest dwellers.
Bullfrogs are significantly larger than their closest New England relatives like Green Frogs and Wood Frogs, and completely lack the fold-like ridges that run down the backs of Green Frogs.
Unlike the green frog which has prominent ridges running down its back, the pickerel frog's back is smooth between its square spots.
Unlike green frogs which have prominent ridges running down their backs, northern leopard frogs have smooth backs with only faint ridges.
Unlike green frogs which have distinct ridges running down their backs and venture onto land regularly, mink frogs have smoother backs and stick close to water.
